cards.title: Core idea
cards.body: Before an HTTPS request is answered, the client resolves the hostname with DNS, opens a TCP connection with a three-way handshake, negotiates encryption with a TLS handshake, then sends the HTTP request. Each step costs round trips.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: Systems reuse connections, cache DNS, resume TLS sessions and use CDNs to cut latency. TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP trades that for speed. HTTP/2 multiplexes over one TCP connection but suffers head-of-line blocking on packet loss; HTTP/3 over QUIC orders each stream independently.

questions.q: How many round trips for a cold HTTPS request?
questions.a: DNS (0 if cached) plus 1 for TCP, 1 for TLS 1.3 (2 for TLS 1.2), and 1 for the HTTP request.

questions.q: What causes 'cannot assign requested address' under load?
questions.a: Ephemeral port exhaustion from a new TCP connection per request leaving TIME_WAIT sockets. Use keep-alive and pooling.
TLS is the encryption and identity layer; HTTPS is HTTP sent over TLS.
